html:
The Chango were fishing peoples of the desert coast of northern Chile and southern Peru, from about Arica south to Coquimbo. They lived by the sea: they hunted sea lions, fished and gathered shellfish, and went out on rafts made of inflated sea lion skins. They traded dried fish with the farming peoples inland, such as the Atacameños, and later with the Inca and Spanish towns.

Spanish writers used "Chango" as a loose name, and scholars still debate whether it meant one people or several coastal groups. They followed a very old way of life on this coast, where the Chinchorro fishers had made mummies thousands of years earlier. Over the colonial period they mixed into the wider population and were often said to have died out, but people of Chango descent remain, and Chile recognised the Chango as an Indigenous people in 2020.
